lesson.title: Who's In Charge of the Internet's Address Book
lesson.summary: ICANN is the nonprofit that coordinates the internet's globally unique identifiers, domain names and IP address blocks, so that no two organizations anywhere in the world are ever handed the same one.
lesson.body:
The Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers, or ICANN, is a nonprofit organization founded in 1998 whose job is to coordinate the internet's globally unique identifier systems: the domain name system and the allocation of IP address space. This is a fundamentally different kind of job from the standards bodies covered in earlier chapters. The IETF, IEEE, and ISO write down the technical rules for how something like an IP address should be formatted and used, while ICANN's role is operational: making sure that once those rules exist, no two organizations anywhere in the world are ever accidentally handed the exact same address or domain name.

ICANN grew out of a set of coordination functions collectively called IANA, the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority, which had been managed under contract with the United States government's National Telecommunications and Information Administration since the early years of the internet. ICANN was created in 1998 to take over this role in a more open, multistakeholder way, bringing together technical experts, businesses, governments, and civil society groups in its decision making. In October 2016, the US government's contractual oversight of the IANA functions formally ended, and stewardship transitioned fully to the global multistakeholder community that ICANN coordinates, a change that had been planned and negotiated for years beforehand.

The IP address allocation piece connects directly to what an IP address actually is. ICANN, through the IANA function it operates, allocates large blocks of IP address space to five Regional Internet Registries: ARIN for North America, RIPE NCC for Europe and the Middle East, APNIC for Asia and the Pacific, LACNIC for Latin America and the Caribbean, and AFRINIC for Africa. Each registry then allocates smaller blocks to internet service providers within its region, and each ISP in turn assigns individual addresses, or small blocks, to its customers. When your home router receives an IP address from your ISP, it is the last, smallest step in a chain of delegation that starts with ICANN. The same coordinating role applies to domain names: ICANN oversees the DNS root zone and decides which top-level domains, such as .com, .org, or country codes like .uk, are allowed to exist and which organizations are authorized to operate them.

It is worth being precise about what ICANN does not do. It does not write the technical specification for how IP addressing or DNS lookups work, since that is IETF territory documented in RFCs, and it does not certify hardware the way IEEE does. Its job is closer to a global registrar and record keeper, making sure the standards other organizations write can actually be deployed at internet scale without collisions.

The reason this coordination matters becomes obvious the moment you imagine it missing. If two different companies were both handed the same IP address block, routers around the world would have no reliable way to know which one a given packet should actually reach, and the same problem would occur if two organizations were both allowed to run the .com top-level domain. Technical standards define the rules of the road, but a coordinating authority like ICANN is what keeps every driver from being issued the same license plate.
